---
title: "Quality control"
---

Before comparing conditions, check whether the samples behave as you expect.
Start with the acquisition and identification metrics recorded by SpectroMesa,
then check quantity distributions, coverage, and sample relationships.

This guide uses the HepG2 DIA demo and the sample assignments from
[Preparing data](preparing-data.html). The examples run on the actual database
when this page is built.

## 1. Start with the prepared data

If you already have `vault`, `sample_info`, `source_id`, and `se` from the previous
guide, reopen the vault if needed and reattach the sample metadata. To run this
article independently, recreate those objects below.

```{r setup, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ProteoVaultR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
    dev.args = list(bg = "white")
)
```

```{r prepare-qc}
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR", unset = "demo-data")
vault <- open_vault(
    path = file.path(data_dir, "hepg2_ifna-dia.proteovault.duckdb")
)

sample_info <- tibble::tribble(
    ~sample_name,   ~sample_id, ~condition,
    "Control_R1",  "Ctrl1",    "Control",
    "Control_R2",  "Ctrl2",    "Control",
    "Control_R3",  "Ctrl3",    "Control",
    "IFNa_12h_R1", "IFNa1",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R2", "IFNa2",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R3", "IFNa3",    "IFNa"
) %>%
    mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Control", "IFNa")))
vault <- set_sample_metadata(vault, sample_info)
method <- "matrix"
source_id <- resolve_quant_source(vault, level = "protein_group", method = method)
se <- as_summarized_experiment(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    source_id = source_id,
    method = method,
    samples = sample_info$sample_name
)
quantity <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(se, "quantity")
se
```

Here, `matrix` contains the imported DIA-NN protein-group matrix values, which
may already include upstream normalization. We use these same measurements for
the protein-level distribution, coverage, and PCA checks below.

## 2. Check acquisition quality

Start with the QC metrics imported from the pipeline. The inventory shows which
layers are present in this database:

```{r qc-inventory}
qc <- tbl_qc_metrics(vault)
qc %>%
    group_by(layer) %>%
    summarise(metrics = n_distinct(metric_name), .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(layer) %>%
    collect() %>%
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("QC layer", "Distinct metrics"))
```

### 2.1. Compare MS2 scan counts

Compare the number of MS2 scans collected in each run:

```{r ms2-scans, fig.alt="Bar chart comparing MS2 scan counts across the six samples."}
plot_qc_metric(vault, "ms2_scan_count")
```

A lower scan count can help explain a coverage difference. Check the run's
`acquisition_duration` as well before concluding that acquisition was incomplete.

### 2.2. Compare signal levels

Total ion current is the sum of peak intensities within each spectrum.
Compare its distribution across runs to look for shifts in signal:

```{r total-ion-current, fig.alt="Percentile boxes comparing per-spectrum total ion current across the six samples."}
plot_qc_boxplot(vault, "total_ion_current")
```

A shift may reflect sample loading, instrument response, or sample composition.
Read it alongside the scan counts and quantity distributions.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Reading QC boxes:** `plot_qc_boxplot()` uses the stored percentiles. The line
marks the median, the box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles, and the whiskers
span the 5th to 95th percentiles. Individual observations and outliers are not shown.
:::

## 3. Check identification quality

The `psm_features` layer contains summaries of the MSFragger search candidates
processed by MSBooster.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Search candidates:** These PSM counts and feature distributions describe the
candidates supplied for rescoring, before final FDR filtering. A target label does
not by itself mean that a PSM is a confident identification.
:::

### 3.1. Compare PSM counts

Start with the number of peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) in each sample:

```{r psm-counts, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt="Grouped bar chart comparing search-candidate PSM counts across samples by target and decoy label."}
plot_qc_metric(vault, "feature_psm_count")
```

`all` is the combined count; `target`, `decoy`, and `unknown` divide candidates by
their recorded labels. Compare counts across replicates, and investigate a sample
with fewer candidates alongside its acquisition and signal checks.

### 3.2. Inspect mass accuracy

Signed precursor mass error is reported in parts per million (ppm):

```{r mass-error, fig.alt="Percentile boxes comparing signed precursor mass error for target and decoy search candidates across samples."}
plot_qc_boxplot(vault, "feature_mass_error_ppm_signed")
```

Check whether the distributions are centered near zero. A shift above or below
zero can reveal a systematic mass offset; a wider distribution shows more variable
errors. Compare these patterns across replicates.

### 3.3. Inspect spectral agreement

MSBooster's weighted spectral entropy measures agreement between observed and
predicted fragment intensities. Higher scores indicate closer agreement; the
weighting means the score is not restricted to a 0–1 scale. See the
[MSBooster feature definitions](https://github.com/Nesvilab/MSBooster#calculated-features).

```{r spectral-agreement, fig.alt="Percentile boxes comparing weighted spectral entropy for target and decoy search candidates across samples."}
plot_qc_boxplot(vault, "feature_weighted_spectral_entropy")
```

In this demo, targets have higher scores than decoys. Check that this pattern is
consistent across replicates, and investigate a sample whose target distribution
shifts toward the decoy distribution.

### 3.4. Inspect retention-time agreement

`feature_delta_rt_loess` summarizes the deviation between observed and predicted
retention times after LOESS calibration. Smaller deviations indicate closer
agreement. MSBooster reports this feature in predicted RT units, rather than
minutes; see its [feature definitions](https://github.com/Nesvilab/MSBooster#calculated-features).

```{r retention-time-agreement, fig.alt="Percentile boxes comparing calibrated retention-time deviations for target and decoy search candidates across samples."}
plot_qc_boxplot(vault, "feature_delta_rt_loess")
```

Targets show smaller deviations than decoys in this demo. Look for unusually
large or variable target deviations, and review them together with spectral
agreement rather than treating either feature as a standalone quality cutoff.

## 4. Compare quantity distributions

Next, inspect the quantities that will be used for analysis. Start at the
precursor level, then look at the protein groups summarized from those signals.

### 4.1. Precursor quantities

By default, this plots the imported DIA-NN precursor matrix:

```{r precursor-quantity-distributions, fig.alt="Boxplots of positive log2 precursor quantities for the six HepG2 samples."}
plot_precursor_quantity_distribution(vault)
```

### 4.2. Protein-group quantities

Compare the same samples at the protein-group level:

```{r quantity-distributions, fig.alt="Boxplots of positive log2 protein-group quantities for the six HepG2 samples."}
plot_protein_quantity_distribution(vault)
```

Compare the middle of each distribution and its spread. A sample with a different
signal level or a much wider distribution deserves a closer look, especially if
its other QC measures also differ. Checking both levels can help you see whether
a change is already present in the precursor signals or is more apparent after
protein-group summarization.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**A plotting scale:** These plots take log2 of positive quantities for display and
omit missing and nonpositive values. They do not change the assay stored in `se`
or the database. Similar-looking distributions alone do not establish good quality.
:::

## 5. Check coverage and missing values

### 5.1. Count quantified protein groups

Count the groups with a positive quantity in each sample:

```{r quantified-counts}
counts <- summarize_quantified_counts(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    source_id = source_id,
    method = method
)
counts %>%
    select(sample_name, quantified_count) %>%
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample", "Quantified protein groups"))
```

A lower count can reflect less signal, incomplete acquisition, or a difference
in the sample itself. Interpret the counts alongside the distributions and
acquisition metrics rather than using one count as an exclusion rule.

### 5.2. Inspect missing and zero quantities

Missing measurements and recorded zeros are different. Keep them separate in
this summary; percentages use all protein groups in the selected matrix.

```{r missingness-summary}
tibble::tibble(
    sample = sample_info$sample_id,
    missing = colSums(is.na(quantity)),
    missing_percent = 100 * colMeans(is.na(quantity)),
    zero = colSums(quantity == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Sample", "Missing", "Missing (%)", "Zeros"),
        digits = 2
    )
```

### 5.3. Check consistency across samples

How many groups are quantified in all six samples, and how many appear in only
some? Summarize the number of samples with a positive quantity for each group:

```{r coverage-plot, fig.alt="Bar chart showing how many protein groups have positive quantities in each number of samples."}
coverage <- summarize_quantification_coverage(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    source_id = source_id,
    method = method
)
coverage %>%
    count(n_samples, name = "protein_groups") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = n_samples, y = protein_groups)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#4E9DA6", colour = "black") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:ncol(quantity)) +
    labs(x = "Samples with a positive quantity", y = "Protein groups") +
    theme_boutroslab()
```

Groups measured consistently are convenient for comparing samples. Groups seen
in only part of the cohort can still be biologically useful; their missingness
needs consideration in the later analysis.

## 6. Compare samples with PCA

Finally, inspect overall sample relationships. Use protein groups with positive,
finite quantities in every sample, and remove constant rows. This gives PCA a
shared set of features without filling missing values.

```{r prepare-sample-comparison}
log_quantity <- quantity
log_quantity[!is.finite(log_quantity) | log_quantity <= 0] <- NA_real_
log_quantity <- log2(log_quantity)
complete <- rowSums(is.finite(log_quantity)) == ncol(log_quantity)
comparison <- log_quantity[complete, , drop = FALSE]
comparison <- comparison[apply(comparison, 1, stats::var) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
nrow(comparison)
```

The result is the number of protein groups retained for PCA. `quantity` and the
`quantity` assay in `se` remain unchanged.

::: {.alert .alert-warning role="note"}
**A selected view of the data:** Complete-case plots leave out groups with missing
or nonpositive values. They can therefore miss problems that are visible in the
coverage checks. This selection is for these diagnostic plots, not a decision to
drop those groups from every later analysis.
:::

Transpose the matrix so samples are observations, then center each protein
group's log2 quantities. Here we keep their existing relative variances rather
than scaling every group
to unit variance. See [the R PCA documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/prcomp.html)
for these options.

```{r sample-pca, fig.alt="PCA scores for the six HepG2 samples, colored by control or IFNa condition and labeled by sample."}
pca <- stats::prcomp(t(comparison), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
variance_percent <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
pca_samples <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]) %>%
    mutate(
        sample_id = sample_info$sample_id,
        condition = sample_info$condition
    )
ggplot(pca_samples, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = condition)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = sample_id), vjust = -0.8,
        size = 11 / (72.27 / 25.4), fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "#4E9DA6", IFNa = "#D98C70")) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
    labs(
        x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", variance_percent[1]),
        y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", variance_percent[2]),
        colour = "Condition"
    ) +
    theme_boutroslab()
```

In this demo, the conditions separate along PC1, while variation among replicates
is visible along PC2. Check whether replicates cluster together and whether a
sample lies apart from the others. Separation between control and IFNα samples
may reflect the treatment response. It is not, by itself, a reason to exclude samples.

## 7. Decide what to do next

Consider these checks together. A sample with lower coverage, a shifted quantity
distribution, and unusual acquisition or identification metrics warrants more
investigation than one that differs in a single plot. Use preparation notes and acquisition records
to help distinguish technical problems from biological variation.

Record any sample exclusions and the evidence supporting them. The code in this
guide does not exclude samples, normalize the assay, or impute missing values.
Those choices come after reviewing the QC results.

```{r close-vault}
close_vault(vault)
vault
```

Keep the prepared `se` object. Next, see [Normalization](normalization.html)
to decide whether an additional adjustment is useful before handling missing
values and testing differences between conditions.
